books.section: American Revolution and the New Nation (1775–1787)

stimulus.source_note: Table compiled from the grounding books; see grounding.
stimulus.text:
| Year | Turning point | What changed |
| 1754 | Seven Years' War begins in North America | Britain and France fight for the continent; the colonies are drawn into an imperial war |
| 1763 | Treaty of Paris ends the war | France loses Canada and its lands east of the Mississippi; Britain takes on a huge war debt |
| 1763 | Proclamation of 1763 | Settlement west of the Appalachians is forbidden; the age of salutary neglect ends |
| 1765–1773 | Stamp Act, Townshend duties, Boston Tea Party | Parliament taxes the colonies for revenue; colonists resist, then organize |
| 1776 | Declaration of Independence | The colonies break with Britain and claim government rests on the consent of the governed |
| 1783 | Treaty of Paris ends the Revolution | Britain recognizes American independence; the new nation holds the land to the Mississippi |
| 1787–1789 | Constitution written and ratified | The weak Articles give way to a stronger federal government |
| 1800 | Election of Thomas Jefferson | Power passes peacefully from one party to another for the first time |

source: original; stimulus is an original data table compiled from the grounding books
stem: The table traces the period from the Seven Years' War to the election of 1800. Which of the following best describes a major continuity across the whole period?

options.text: The colonies' elected assemblies steadily lost power until the Constitution abolished them in 1789.
options.misconception: The assemblies were never abolished; state legislatures continued under the Constitution.

options.text: Native American nations kept the same leverage over Britain and the United States that they had held before 1763.
options.misconception: The removal of France destroyed the Native nations' ability to play empires against each other; their leverage shrank, not held.

options.text: Enslaved people remained in bondage through the Revolution and the founding of the republic, even as the nation proclaimed liberty.
The United States stayed out of European wars entirely, exactly as Washington's Farewell Address had advised.
options.misconception: The young republic was pulled into European conflicts almost at once — the Quasi-War with France in 1798, and the War of 1812 followed soon after.

rationales.A: The assemblies were never abolished; state legislatures continued under the Constitution.
rationales.B: The removal of France destroyed the Native nations' ability to play empires against each other; their leverage shrank, not held.
rationales.C: The Revolution proclaimed that all men are created equal, and the new republic was built on that language — yet slavery survived the war, the Constitution, and the election of 1800. Background: the Constitution protected the slave trade until 1808 and counted enslaved people as three-fifths of a person, and by 1800 enslaved people still worked the fields of the South and the households of the North. The democratic spirit that the books describe inspired change abroad and at home, but it did not give birth to a perfect democracy.
rationales.D: The young republic was pulled into European conflicts almost at once — the Quasi-War with France in 1798, and the War of 1812 followed soon after.
rationales.general:
1. Scan the whole table, 1754 to 1800. Wars end, governments change, parties form — what does not change?
2. Test each option against the full span. Assemblies were never abolished; Native leverage fell after France left; the republic was pulled toward European wars within a decade.
3. Look at what the Revolution promised and what it delivered. The language of liberty was universal, but bondage continued through every turning point on the table.
4. Put it together. The period's deepest continuity is the gap between its ideals and its reality.
Remember: a continuity is not a single event — it is the thing that survives every event on the list.
